lede: George Pitt D'Arcy is the best-documented D'Arcy in this archive and has never had a page. He is also the join on which the whole Australian descent hangs: if he is Robert D'Arcy's son, the line runs from a Royal Engineer at Chatham to a convict ship and Queensland. That he was Robert's son has been a family tree's assertion and nothing else — until this.

notice.paper: Salisbury and Winchester Journal, Monday 23 September 1805, page 3
notice.also: The same London report of 16 September was carried by the Hampshire Telegraph on the same day.
notice.text: Lately, Captain GEORGE D'ARCY, [of] the [—] foot, SON [of] LIEUT. COLONEL D'ARCY, [to] MISS LUDLAM, OF GUERNSEY.
notice.ocr: The scan is damaged and the small connecting words are lost — the regiment's number reads only as “tiie foot”. What survives is the structure of an ordinary marriage notice of the period, and the three facts in it: the groom's name and rank, his father's rank, and the bride.

why: It is the first record that makes him anyone's son.
Every other document this archive holds names George Pitt D'Arcy as a husband, a father, an officer or a passenger. None has ever named his father. This one does — not by name, but by rank.
And the rank fits, to the month.

ROBERT D'ARCY WAS GAZETTED LIEUTENANT-COLONEL ON 1 MARCH 1805, vice Nepean, six months before this notice was printed. In September 1805 he was a Lieut.-Colonel of the Royal Engineers, which is exactly what the notice calls the groom's father.
It confirms a tree claim from outside the tree.
The family tree has always said George Pitt D'Arcy married a Miss Ludlam about 1805. A Wiltshire newspaper printed it at the time, and neither knows about the other.
caveat: The notice does not give the father's forename, and this archive has not enumerated every Lieutenant-Colonel D'Arcy serving in 1805 — there were 446 D'Arcy entries in the military collections searched and no cheap way to isolate them. So this is a very strong identification and not a proof. What it is not is an assertion: it is a contemporary printed statement that the man had a father of that rank.
life: Married MISS LUDLAM OF GUERNSEY, as Captain George D'Arcy, son of Lieut.-Colonel D'Arcy
His son FREDERICK ROBERT D'ARCY baptised at Chatham — mother MARY
“a party of the 39th regiment, under the command of Major D'Arcy”, going to the assistance of the yeomanry in Ireland with Dominick Browne Esq.
“the detachment of the 39th regiment quartered in that town, under the command of Major D'Arcy”, near Cork
His daughter CHARLOTTE baptised at Chatham — “Bt: Major 39th Foot”, mother MARIA
Embarked the convict ship ENGLAND commanding a detachment of the 39th, with Mrs D'Arcy and family in the cabin

wives.head: Two wives, and only one of them found
wives.first: MISS LUDLAM of Guernsey, married about September 1805 — now documented. The Chatham baptism of 1811 gives Frederick Robert's mother as MARY, so she was very probably Mary Ludlam.
wives.second: MARIA WHITE, whom the tree marries him to in County Wicklow about 1819, and who is the Maria of the 1826 baptism. Searched in the Irish and British press for 1816–1823 and not found. The newspapers do place him in Ireland with the 39th in 1820 and 1822, which is the right country at nearly the right time — but that is context, not a record.

matters: This is why the archive cares. Frederick Robert D'Arcy, baptised Chatham 1811 to George and MARY, and Charlotte, baptised Chatham 1826 to George and MARIA, are half-brother and half-sister — and the 1805 notice is the first evidence from outside the family that there were two marriages at all.
